pause.name: Pause
pause.description: Suppress the bridge's effect on its lights for a short time, then resume automatically. For radio-airtime contention: nothing about what the lights should look like has changed, so the session (if any) is left alone and carries on once the pause ends.

seconds.name: Seconds
seconds.description: How long to pause for. 0 uses a healthy default (a couple of seconds).

resume.name: Resume
resume.description: Cancel an in-progress pause early. No effect if nothing is paused, or if a release is in progress.

release.name: Release
release.description: Stop driving the lights until a new session genuinely begins. For an intent change such as a lighting sweep: discards the pending restore target so the lights stay as the caller set them, asks a compliant TV to stop via the stream-active flag, and forces the same clean teardown if it doesn't comply within the grace period.

seconds.name: Seconds
seconds.description: Grace period to wait for the TV to comply before forcing it. 0 uses a healthy default (a couple of seconds).

settle_seconds.name: Settle seconds
settle_seconds.description: Optional: block this call for this long before returning, after the release has already taken effect. Gives a command that was already mid-send when release() was called time to actually land before your own sweep (e.g. light.turn_off) starts competing for the same radio. 0 (default) skips this entirely.

data_description.pair_now: Opens a 60-second pairing window after saving.
data_description.bind_ip: Leave blank to use the auto-detected HA host IP. Set to a secondary IP address (e.g. a macvlan interface) to bind the bridge's HTTP, HTTPS and DTLS servers to that address only, freeing ports 80 and 443 on the primary IP for Home Assistant, Traefik or Nginx.
data_description.http_mode: Where the Hue REST API is served. Automatic: uses Home Assistant's own web server when it listens on port 80 without HTTPS (Settings → System → Network, HA 2026.8+), otherwise a standalone server on port 80. Change only if the automatic choice is wrong.
data_description.https_enabled: Opens an HTTPS server on port 443 with a Hue-bridge-style certificate, as the official Hue Sync app expects (e.g. on Samsung TVs). Not needed for Philips Ambilight TVs. Untested with a real Hue Sync app so far — see the README.

error.https_port_used_by_ha: Home Assistant's own web server uses port 443. Move it off 443 (Settings → System → Network), or set a separate bind IP for the bridge.

https_port_used_by_ha.title: Hue Sync app support can't use port 443
https_port_used_by_ha.description:
Hue Sync app support is enabled, but Home Assistant's own web server listens on port {port}, and the Hue Sync app only connects to that port. Ambilight keeps working.

To fix it, either move Home Assistant's web server off port {port} (Settings → System → Network), or give the bridge its own IP address with the **Bind IP address** option (Container/Core installs; Home Assistant must then listen on its main IP only). Otherwise, turn Hue Sync app support off in the integration's options.

https_port_unavailable.title: Hue Sync app support can't open port 443
https_port_unavailable.description:
Hue Sync app support is enabled, but port {port} could not be opened: {error}. Ambilight keeps working.

Another service (for example a reverse proxy add-on) probably holds the port. Free it, or give the bridge its own IP address with the **Bind IP address** option, then reload the integration. Otherwise, turn Hue Sync app support off in the integration's options.
